result.summary:
I searched the web and read the full text or abstracts of the key works: BCCP in both the arXiv and Political Analysis versions, the pintervals paper (arXiv 2601.03994), Wang et al. 2023 (BFQR, full text), Sadinle, Lei and Wasserman 2019 (full text), Kandinsky CP, Izbicki et al. 2020, Yi et al. 2025, and the 2025-2026 preprints on response bins, label shift, tail-specific intervals and long-tailed conformal classification. I found no paper or package that already proposes conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds for a continuous outcome, or proves their size-optimality. The method and its framing therefore survive. Compared with cycle 1, the positioning is now mostly honest: Mondrian/BCCP validity is not claimed, Proposition 2 is credited as the per-stratum form of known level-set results, Kiyani, Barber et al. 2023 and Podkopaev & Ramdas are cited, the floor rule is disclaimed, and the gain over S-NCP is stated to be small.

Several credit and attribution errors remain. A hostile reviewer, especially one of the BCCP or BFQR authors, would catch them, and some are factual misstatements about other people's papers:
(1) Proposition 3 is presented as a new proof, but Sadinle et al. (2019, Theorems 14 and 16) already prove, with rates, that a plug-in classifier calibrated by split conformal within each class converges to the class-specific oracle. Sadinle et al. also characterise the null region (empty sets) of the class-specific oracle and give remedies; this was requested in cycle 1 and has still not been done.
(2) The manuscript says twice that Randahl et al. note the BCCP guarantee holds for any score. The published BCCP article does not say this. The source is the pintervals paper and package, which also offer heteroscedastic and custom scores for BCCP. That paper is not cited, and the abstract and highlights still compare against an unqualified "bin-conditional conformal prediction" (cycle-1 C1-02 items 1 and 3, inadequately fixed).
(3) Wang et al. 2023 predates BCCP and already evaluates an equal-level, Y-binned label-conditional CQR baseline (LCQR), which is the paper's S-CQR. The related-work paragraph on BFQR introduces the method twice and misdescribes Wang et al.'s Fig. 1. Wang et al.'s Theorem 3.1 (equalized versus outcome-conditional coverage) is not credited in Section 3.2.
(4) The directly analogous classification literature on long-tailed conformal prediction is missing: Ding, Fermanian & Salmon (ICLR 2026); Liu, Huang & Ong (AAAI 2026); Bhattacharyya, Ding & Barber (arXiv 2606.28598, which characterises the smallest sets under weighted class-group coverage). It is relevant to the motivation, to Proposition 2 and to the floor variant.
(5) The highlights and abstract overstate what is new and what was found: "guarantees coverage of rare, extreme outcomes" although top-1% coverage is 0.736, and "smallest ... on 31 datasets".

None of these issues needs a new experiment. All can be fixed in the text within a day. Once they are fixed, I consider the novelty positioning ready for ESWA submission. The realistic residual risk is an editor judging the methodological increment over BCCP plus S-NCP as modest; the paper already discloses this.

issues.title: Proposition 3 (asymptotic size-optimality of the plug-in procedure) is the continuous-outcome counterpart of Sadinle et al. (2019) Theorems 14 and 16, which are not credited
issues.evidence: manuscript_filled.md line 24 (contribution 1): "We prove that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically size-optimal under uniform consistency of the density estimate (Proposition 3)." Line 140: "its proof (Appendix A) follows the plug-in arguments of @lei2013distribution and @izbicki2022cdsplit". The abstract (line 8) also says "We show ... that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically optimal". Sadinle, Lei & Wasserman (JASA 2019; arXiv 1609.00451v2, Section 4) cover exactly the class-specific (label-conditional) case. Their Theorem 14 gives a rate bound P_y(Ĉ_y Δ C*_y) ≤ c(γ_n + sqrt(log n / n)) for the plug-in class-specific classifier under sup-norm consistency of p̂ and a margin condition at t_y. Their Theorem 16 states that the same result holds for the split-conformal version, which calibrates thresholds within each class (their Eq. 7, "label validity" in Vovk's terms). Proposition 3 is this result with Lebesgue measure in place of counting measure. It is weaker, since it gives no rate. src/02_theory.md line 58 credits only the marginal level-set results. The manuscript cites Sadinle only for the oracle characterisation (Proposition 2).
issues.corrective_action: In 02_theory.md line 58 (before Proposition 3), add: "For classification with class-specific coverage, @sadinle2019least [Thms 14 and 16] prove the corresponding consistency, with rates, for the split-conformal plug-in classifier calibrated within each class; Proposition 3 is its counterpart for a continuous outcome and fixed strata, stated without rates." In 01_intro.md line 11, replace "We prove that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically size-optimal" with "We show, following the class-specific results of @sadinle2019least, that their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically size-optimal". Change "We show" in the abstract to "We extend known level-set results to show" (or similar). Add the same credit to the cover-letter contribution 1 and to the Section 8 sentence "their plug-in conformal version is asymptotically optimal".

issues.title: BCCP misattributed and under-described: the published BCCP article never states validity 'for any score'; the score-agnostic reference implementation (pintervals) is not cited; the headline comparator is still unqualified
issues.evidence: src/01_intro.md line 9, src/015_related.md line 21 and src/02_theory.md line 33 (manuscript_filled.md lines 52 and 115) state that "@randahl2026bin note that it holds for any score" / "note that the bin-wise guarantee holds for any score". I checked the Political Analysis 34(1):96-108 full text (Cambridge core reader) and arXiv 2410.14507v2. BCCP's guarantee is stated for its algorithm with the absolute prediction error. The phrase 'any measure of dissimilarity' appears only in the generic split-conformal background, and no score other than the absolute error is discussed. The score-agnostic statement is in the pintervals paper (Randahl, Hjort & Williams, arXiv 2601.03994, Jan 2026, Section 2.1 and the pinterval_bccp description). That paper says pinterval_bccp takes the same score options as pinterval_conformal: absolute (default), relative, zero-adjusted relative, heterogeneous and raw errors, or a user-supplied custom score. It also says both union and contiguized forms 'achieve at least the desired coverage level'. The bib already contains randahl2026pintervals (CRAN, line 1361), but no manuscript source cites it (grep of manuscript/src returns nothing). So BCCP's own implementation already supports a heteroscedastic, S-NCP-like score and could take the density score as a custom function. The abstract (line 8), however, says "smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction on 24 of 31 datasets", and highlight 4 / Section 7.1 speak of BCCP without naming the score. Cycle-1 C1-02 asked to "Rename ... 'BCCP with the absolute-residual score'" and to "Describe BCCP accurately ... score-agnostic, with heteroscedastic scores in its reference implementation". Response_01 C1-02 does not report doing either. The fix is inadequate.
issues.corrective_action: (a) Delete "@randahl2026bin note that it holds for any score" in all three places. Replace with: "the guarantee holds for any score (it is the Mondrian argument), and the reference implementation of BCCP [@randahl2026pintervals; Randahl, Hjort & Williams, arXiv:2601.03994] accepts absolute, relative, heterogeneous and user-supplied scores". Add the arXiv paper to the bib. (b) In Section 2.2 / 5.4, say that BCCP with pintervals' heterogeneous score is close in spirit to S-NCP, and that SDLC can be viewed as BCCP with a particular custom score. The contribution is the choice and theory of that score, not a new calibration rule. (c) In the abstract, write "smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction with the absolute-residual score (BCCP) on 24 of 31 datasets". Use the same qualifier in highlight 4, Section 7.1 and the cover letter, as already done in Section 8.

issues.title: Wang et al. (2023) credited inaccurately: priority, the existing equal-level Y-binned CQR baseline (LCQR = S-CQR), a duplicated BFQR introduction, a misdescribed figure, and their Theorem 3.1
issues.evidence: (i) Priority. src/01_intro.md line 9: "@randahl2026bin proposed it as bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP)". Wang et al. (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2311.02243, Nov 2023) calibrate within Y-bins one year before BCCP (arXiv 2410.14507, Oct 2024). They also describe their method as "a variant of Mondrian conformal prediction" (Sec. 4.2). (ii) LCQR. Wang et al. Sec. 5.1 compares against "Label-conditional Conformalized Quantile Regression (LCQR) ... designed for classification ... We adapt it to regression tasks". Sec. 5.2.2 explains its width: "enforcing all bins to reach the same high coverage rates generates prediction results with little useful information". That is Y-binned CQR at a common level, i.e. the S-CQR baseline here. manuscript_filled.md line 15 of Section 5.4 says only that S-CQR "is related to the binned calibration of @wang2023equal but omits its level optimisation". (iii) Duplication. manuscript_filled.md line 50 introduces BFQR twice: "their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) splits $Y$ into equal-mass bins ..." and two sentences later "Their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) forms equal-mass bins ..." (src/015_related.md line 19). (iv) Fig. 1. The same paragraph says Wang et al. "illustrate that standard methods mis-cover the head and tail bins of the outcome". Their Fig. 1 shows coverage differences between gender groups within the head and tail salary bins under equalized coverage, not overall mis-coverage of those bins. (v) Theorem 3.1. Wang et al.'s Theorem 3.1 (Mutual Exclusivity) shows that coverage equalised across X-defined groups and coverage equalised conditionally on Y cannot both hold when A and V depend on Y. Section 3 of their paper states that equalized coverage "fails to ensure equal coverage conditional on Y, especially for extreme values of Y". This is the qualitative statement of manuscript Section 3.2 ("Covariate-conditional validity does not imply target-conditional validity"), but Section 3.2 cites Wang et al. only for empirical under-coverage (line 89).
issues.corrective_action: (i) In 01_intro.md line 9, write: "@wang2023equal calibrate within bins of the outcome to equalise coverage across groups, and @randahl2026bin proposed bin-conditional conformal prediction (BCCP) for the skewed distribution of conflict fatalities." (ii) In Section 5.4, add: "S-CQR with a common level coincides with the label-conditional CQR (LCQR) baseline of @wang2023equal, who report it to be wide." (iii) Merge the two BFQR sentences in 015_related.md line 19 into one description. (iv) Replace the Fig. 1 description with: "and they show that equalized coverage leaves coverage unequal across groups within the head and tail bins of the outcome". (v) In Section 3.2 after Proposition 1, add: "@wang2023equal [Thm 3.1] show that equal coverage across covariate-defined groups and equal coverage conditional on $Y$ are mutually exclusive; Proposition 1 quantifies the analogous gap for the oracle covariate-conditional set."

issues.title: Missing the directly analogous literature on conformal prediction for long-tailed (imbalanced) classification, including recent optimal-set results under class-group coverage and threshold interpolation
issues.evidence:
The manuscript positions itself as the regression counterpart of label-conditional coverage (lines 46, 77). It does not cite the 2025-2026 work on conformal prediction for long-tailed classification, which addresses the same problem (marginal sets under-cover rare labels) for discrete labels:
- Ding, Fermanian & Salmon, 'Conformal prediction for long-tailed classification' (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2507.06867). It introduces macro-coverage, an approximately optimal 'prevalence-adjusted softmax' score, and a procedure that linearly interpolates between marginal and class-conditional conformal thresholds.
- Liu, Huang & Ong, 'Conformal prediction meets long-tail classification' (AAAI 2026, vol. 40, pp. 23828-23836; arXiv 2508.11345).
- Bhattacharyya, Ding & Barber, 'Conformal prediction with macro-coverage guarantees' (arXiv 2606.28598, June 2026). It gives finite-sample guarantees for weighted averages of group-conditional coverages over label groupings and 'characterize[s] the form of the smallest prediction sets' with a matching score, connected explicitly to Sadinle et al.
The grep of references_verified.bib finds none of these. They matter for three passages:
(a) The motivation (line 20) and Section 2.3 claim (line 58) that guarantees for rare targets 'have so far come from conflict forecasting and fair regression'.
(b) Proposition 2, whose classification analogues now include weighted label-group objectives.
(c) The floor variant (line 182). Threshold interpolation between marginal and class-conditional calibration is a published compromise, and the floor rule credits only @wang2023equal and @kiyani2024length.
issues.corrective_action: Add two or three sentences to Section 2.2 (classification paragraph, src/015_related.md line 15): "In long-tailed classification, marginal sets under-cover rare classes in the same way [Ding, Fermanian & Salmon 2026; Liu, Huang & Ong 2026]; proposed remedies interpolate between marginal and class-conditional thresholds or target macro-coverage, the unweighted average of class-conditional coverages, for which the smallest sets and a matching score have been characterised [Bhattacharyya, Ding & Barber 2026]." In Section 4.5, add Ding et al. (threshold interpolation) as a principled alternative to the floor rule. In Section 7.3, name macro-coverage over strata, with the score $f(y|x)/f_Y(y)$ suggested by those results, as an untested intermediate guarantee. Verify all three entries on DBLP, the AAAI proceedings and arXiv before adding them to references_verified.bib.

issues.title: Empty sets and the 'coverage reallocation' remark do not credit Sadinle et al.'s null-region analysis (cycle-1 C1-04 item 5 not implemented)
issues.evidence: manuscript_filled.md line 152 derives that the oracle set "is empty whenever $t_k\sigma(x)>\max g$" and reports that SDLC returns empty sets for 0.36% of test points (line 140; Table 2 'Empty %' 0.36 vs S-NCP 0.07). Sadinle et al. (2019, Sec. 2.2 after Theorem 6, and Sec. 3) show that the class-specific level-set oracle has a 'null region' {x: H(x)=∅}. They give a sufficient condition for its absence (Σ_y t_y ≤ 1) and propose two principled remedies, including 'accretive completion' (Algorithm 1), which also applies to the split-conformal estimator. Cycle-1 review C1-04 item 5 asked to "Discuss Sadinle et al.'s null-region remedies". The response_01 entry for C1-04 does not mention it, and grep for 'null region|accretive' in manuscript/src returns nothing.
issues.corrective_action: In Section 4.2 ('Coverage is reallocated across inputs'), add: "Empty sets are the regression counterpart of the null region of class-specific level sets [@sadinle2019least, Sec. 3], who show that it is generic and propose filling it (accretive completion) at a controlled cost in size." In Section 7.2 item 3 or the limitations, name a simple remedy that keeps validity: return the hull of the stratum pieces closest to $\hat\mu(x)$, or $[\hat\mu(x)\pm\epsilon]$, for empty sets. Adding points never lowers coverage, so this preserves (5). An optional evaluation from cache is not required.

issues.title: Highlights and abstract overstate novelty and results
issues.evidence:
src/highlights.md:
- Line 4: "Calibrating within target strata guarantees coverage of rare, extreme outcomes." Two problems. The device is established Mondrian/BCCP calibration, and the paper explicitly does not claim it (lines 22, 52). And the guarantee does not extend to extreme outcomes beyond the calibrated strata: SDLC covers 0.736 of the top 1% (Table 2), and line 73 says "its coverage remains below the nominal level for every method".
- Line 5: "Stratum-wise density level sets are the smallest stratum-valid prediction sets" reads as a new result. It is the per-stratum form of Sadinle et al. Theorem 6 (see line 46).
- Line 6: "SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets on 31 datasets, confirmed on 17" reads as smallest on each dataset. In fact SDLC is larger than S-NCP on 4 CTR23 datasets (line 271), and the S-NCP and S-HPD geometric-mean CIs include 1 on the held-out data (Table 7: 0.977 [0.940, 1.028], 0.984 [0.963, 1.014]).
- Abstract line 8: "We show that conditional-density level sets ... are the smallest stratum-valid sets" gives no hint that this extends known classification results.
issues.corrective_action:
Rewrite the highlights, each ≤ 85 characters. Suggested wording:
(2) "Stratified (Mondrian) calibration restores coverage in every target stratum"
(3) "Size-optimal stratum-valid sets are density level sets with per-stratum thresholds"
(4) "SDLC gave the smallest stratified sets on average; replicated on 17 held-out sets"
In the abstract, use "Extending level-set results for class-specific coverage, we show ...". Optionally add "with the absolute-residual score" after "bin-conditional conformal prediction" (see the BCCP issue).

issues.title: Contribution 2 claims an 'exact, stratum-exact implementation' with linear cost, but the reported geometry is that of an interpolant, and linear cost is not distinctive
issues.evidence: src/01_intro.md line 12 (manuscript_filled.md line 25): "It has an exact, stratum-exact implementation whose cost is linear in the number of test points." Section 4.4 (line 174) says that size, pieces, hull and alerts are computed numerically: "The reported geometry is therefore that of the stratum-exact set for the piecewise-linear interpolant of $\hat g$." Only coverage membership is exact. Grid error is up to 0.2% in mean size and 1.5% per point (Table S4). Every split-conformal method has cost linear in the number of test points. The cover letter (contribution 2) repeats the claim.
issues.corrective_action: Replace with: "Coverage is evaluated exactly at the observed target, and set geometry is computed stratum-exactly for a piecewise-linear interpolant of the noise density (grid error ≤ 0.2% in mean size), at O(G log K) per test point." Apply the same wording in the cover letter. Do not present linear cost as a contribution.

issues.title: The dedicated tail-alert baseline (TC-LS/TC-H) and the label-shift literature lack standard credits
issues.evidence: Section 5.4 (manuscript_filled.md line 19, src/03_setup.md line 34) introduces the "class-conditional conformal tail classifier" without a citation, and Section 2.3 (line 58) also describes it uncited. It is split-conformal label-conditional calibration of a binary event, i.e. Neyman–Pearson classification with the miss rate controlled by an order statistic of the positives' scores (Lei 2014, Biometrika, 'Classification with confidence', already in the bib as lei2014classification; Sadinle et al. 2019; Tong, Feng & Li 2018, Science Advances 4:eaao1659, the NP umbrella algorithm). Section 2.4 lists regression label-shift methods (yi2025, lee2026split). It omits the recent preprints by Choi (arXiv 2607.02173 and 2609.27976, 2026) on conformal prediction under continuous label shift in regression. The latter shows that exact validity under continuous exponential tilts makes sets unbounded. That directly supports the paper's point (Corollary 1, Table 8) that stratified calibration is exact only for whole-stratum re-weighting.
issues.corrective_action: In Section 5.4, add "[cf. @lei2014classification; @sadinle2019least; Tong et al. 2018]" after "class-conditional conformal tail classifier". Optionally, add one sentence in Section 2.4: "Exact validity under continuous tilts of the target is generally attainable only with unbounded sets [Choi 2026], which is consistent with Corollary 1(ii)-(iii)." Verify each entry before adding it to the bib.

result.summary:
I checked every proof in Appendix A line by line, and the core mathematics is correct. Proposition 1: the conditional law, the derivative sign argument and the table values all check out. I recomputed Eq. (2) by quadrature and got 0.7052, 0.3750 and 0.9487 at R^2 = 0.5 and 0.8617 at R^2 = 0.9, matching the 70.5%, 37.5%, 94.9% and 86.2% in the manuscript. Theorem 1: the rank argument holds with random tie-breaking, the strict upper bound holds, and the r_k > n_k case is right. I also confirmed that the floating-point ceil in conformal_quantile matches exact rational arithmetic for alpha in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} and n_k up to 20,000. Corollary 1 (i)-(iii) is correct, including the chord/convexity total-variation bound and the tanh optimum. Proposition 2's per-stratum Neyman-Pearson proof is correct, and so is the extension to data-dependent sets, because the Lagrangian inequality is linear. The new Proposition 3 is also correct: the order-statistic Lipschitz step, the sign-disagreement bound and the dominated-convergence step via the zero-measure level set all hold. The covariance identity in the Remark is correct.

The implementation matches the equations. The score is -g(z)/s. Thresholds are stratum-specific and use the candidate's stratum (searchsorted with side='right' gives half-open strata). Infinite thresholds give the whole stratum within D, the floor is max(1e-3 sd, 0.05 median|r_oof|), the defensive t2 component has scale IQR/1.349, and the residuals are cross-fitted. The monotone-run geometry reproduces the cell-wise reference; tests/test_ls_exact3.py passes (4/4, run read-only).

The remaining problems are inconsistencies between claims and implementation, not errors in the proofs:
- Out-of-domain handling. The manuscript says Theorem 1's lower bound "applies to the reported coverage" and promises to report the fraction of test targets outside D. That fraction is never reported. For the interval comparators, calibration ignores D while test coverage is clipped to D.
- The positive control of the shift experiment is an arithmetic identity for stratum-wise coverage, so it cannot test Corollary 1(i).
- The cost statement in Algorithm 1 does not match the final algorithm.
- The word "exact" is overstated for the set geometry.
- Proposition 3 is said to "apply" to SDLC although the scale floor and the domain truncation violate its uniform-consistency assumption.
- Highlight 2 still overclaims coverage of extreme outcomes.

None of these needs a new experiment; all can be fixed in the text or by re-analysis from existing result files. I see nothing that would cause desk rejection. The theory is sound once these statements are made precise.

issues.title: Out-of-domain targets: the claim that Theorem 1's lower bound 'applies to the reported coverage' is not exactly true, the promised out-of-D fraction is never reported, and SDLC and the interval comparators handle D differently
issues.evidence: (1) manuscript src/02_theory.md, 'Exact scores and the domain' (rendered line 172), says a target outside D counts as not covered, 'so the lower bound of Theorem 1 applies to the reported coverage'. The same paragraph says 'We report the fraction of test targets outside D and how often q_k=+inf occurs'. No such fraction appears anywhere in manuscript_filled.md or supplementary_filled.md, although it is computed: results/metrics_v3.json has frac_test_out_domain_mean = 0.00025 and frac_test_out_domain_max = 0.00385, and evaluate_from_cache3.py line 143 computes it per run. (2) In the code, coverage is (sc_test <= thr[k]) & part.in_domain(y_test) (ls_exact3.py lines 204 and 323), and metrics.covered() applies '& ind' for every method. When q_k = +inf and Y_test is outside D, the extended-real rule s <= q_k holds, so Theorem 1 counts the point as covered while the code counts it as uncovered. The proof's line 'if r_k>n_k, then q_k=+inf and coverage is one' therefore does not describe the implemented set B_k ∩ D. (3) For the interval comparators (BCCP, S-NCP, S-CQR, S-Res), conformal.interval_method computes calibration scores |y-mu| or |y-mu|/sigma with no domain restriction, so calibration points outside D get finite scores, while test points outside D are counted as uncovered. Their reported stratum coverage can therefore fall below (5) by up to P(Y outside D | Y in B_k). SDLC assigns +inf to calibration points outside D (scores(), line 104), which raises its thresholds accordingly, so the two families are not treated alike. (4) Magnitude, computed from raw_eval_v3/*.jsonl: forest_fires has on average 0.385% of test targets outside D (maximum 2.3% in one split). With about 130 test points and 11.7 upper-stratum test points per split, that is roughly 0.5 points per split, i.e. about 4% of the upper stratum. space_ga has 0.13% and cars 0.10%; 16 datasets have none.
issues.corrective_action: (a) Rewrite the sentence along these lines: 'Theorem 1 applies to the set (4) with the extended-real convention; because every method counts targets outside D as not covered, the reported stratum coverage can fall below (5) by at most P(Y not in D | Y in B_k).' Correct the parenthesis in the proof of Theorem 1, or add a footnote that the implementation reports B_k ∩ D. (b) Report the promised numbers: mean and maximum fraction of test targets outside D, as a per-dataset column in Table S1 (overall mean 0.025%; forest fires 0.385%, about 4% of its upper stratum). Also report the number of runs in which q_k = +inf because the r_k-th calibration score is +inf: n_inf() in evaluate_from_cache3.py counts only r_k > n_k. (c) Either harmonise the methods by assigning +inf calibration scores outside D to the interval comparators as well (a re-evaluation from cache, no refitting), or state explicitly that the comparators' calibration ignores D and that this can only lower their reported coverage.
issues.new_experiment: Optional: re-run evaluate_from_cache3.py with interval-method calibration scores set to +inf outside D, and report whether any number in Tables 2, 5 or 7 changes in the third decimal. This is re-analysis from cache, well under a few CPU hours.

issues.title: The positive control in the shift experiment is an arithmetic identity for stratum-wise coverage, so it cannot confirm Corollary 1(i)
issues.evidence: shift_weights3() (evaluate_from_cache3.py lines 106-115) defines 'pc' weights that are constant within each calibration stratum (5 on the top stratum, 0.5 on the bottom, 1 elsewhere). evaluate() then computes stratum coverage as sum(w*c)/sum(w) within each stratum, which equals the unweighted stratum coverage exactly. Over 7,200 rows of raw_eval_v3, |shift_pc_cal_worst - cal_worst| has a maximum of 6.7e-16. As a result, Table 8 'Positive control: worst stratum' reproduces Table 2 'Worst stratum' for every method, marginal methods included (SCP 0.630 = 0.630, NCP 0.765 = 0.765, DLS 0.660 = 0.660). Section 6.6 nevertheless says: 'Under the positive control ... the stratum-wise coverage of every stratified method was unchanged, as Corollary 1(i) states.' This was the fix for cycle-1 issue C1-18 ('no positive control'), but for stratum-wise coverage it is a tautology, not a check.
issues.corrective_action: State that stratum-wise coverage is unchanged by construction under whole-stratum re-weighting, and remove the 'Positive control: worst stratum' column from Table 8 or mark it 'identical to Table 2 by construction'. Keep the positive-control marginal coverage column, which is informative: it tests the marginal statement of Corollary 1(i), Q-coverage >= 1 - sum_k pi_k alpha_k = 0.9, which stratified methods meet (0.904-0.906) and marginal methods do not (0.838-0.877). Reword Section 6.6 to say this.

issues.title: The cost stated in Algorithm 1 does not match the final monotone-run algorithm
issues.evidence: Algorithm 1 (src/02_theory.md) says: 'Prediction costs O(G log K) per test point for a grid of G standardised points.' The final implementation, ls_exact3.build_sets, loops over K strata and R monotone runs and calls np.interp (a binary search) on each run. Its own docstring (line 238) gives the cost as 'O(K R log G) per test point for R runs instead of O(K G)'. The reference _build_sets_ref is O(KG). Neither is O(G log K).
issues.corrective_action: Replace the statement with: 'after an O(G) precomputation of the R monotone runs of the interpolant of g, prediction costs O(K R log G) per test point (R is the number of monotone pieces, at most twice the number of local extrema of g plus two).' Check that Table S13 is described as timing this algorithm.

issues.title: The implementation is called 'exact', but the reported geometry re-interpolates g on a second, coarser grid
issues.evidence: Introduction, contribution 2: 'It has an exact, stratum-exact implementation'. Cover letter item 2: 'an exact implementation'. In the code, the model g used for the scores is piecewise linear on RobustLSDensity.grid (spacing h/4, up to 2^18 knots; density.py lines 145-160, g_at line 169). The geometry instead interpolates g_at at a different grid LSTable3.zs (1536 core points over the 0.1%-99.9% residual range plus 2x256 log-spaced points; ls_exact3.py lines 41-51). The reported sets are therefore not the sets defined by the score. tests/test_ls_exact3.py::test_membership_matches_exact_rule tolerates 0.2% disagreement. The grid-convergence check is non-monotone for brazilian_houses (did 44990): mean size is 9167.4 with the 512-point core, 9164.9 with 1536 and 9180.2 with 6144 (metrics_v3.json grid_convergence). The 'finest' grid differs from both coarser ones in the same direction, so convergence is not demonstrated there.
issues.corrective_action: Either (a) reword to 'exact coverage rule (scores evaluated at the observed target) and numerically accurate geometry (grid-convergence check, Table S4)' in the introduction, cover letter and Section 4.4; or (b) make the geometry exact for the model by building LSTable3.zs from the model's own knots RobustLSDensity.grid (plus 0). Because the monotone-run algorithm's cost grows only with log G and R, this costs almost nothing per test point, and the sets whose coverage is scored would then coincide with the sets whose size is reported. Option (b) needs only a re-evaluation from cache.

issues.title: The claim that Proposition 3 applies to SDLC ignores the scale floor and the domain truncation
issues.evidence: Section 4.3: 'If Y=mu(X)+sigma(X)eps with eps independent of X, (8) can be consistent, so Proposition 3 applies.' Proposition 3 assumes eps_N = sup_{x,y}|f_hat - f| -> 0. (i) The floor sigma_hat >= 0.05 median|r_oof| does not vanish as N grows, so f_hat is inconsistent wherever sigma(x) falls below it. In the seed-0 caches (raw_contexts/*_0.npz vs raw_contexts_v3 floor_new), sigma_hat sits at the floor for 7.6% of test points on socmob and 3.5% on auction_verification. socmob is also the dataset where SDLC loses most to S-NCP (ratio 1.64, Section 6.9). (ii) The implemented score is +inf outside D, i.e. f_hat = 0 there, while sup_x f(y|x) for y outside D need not tend to 0 when mu(X) is unbounded. (iii) The statement lets 'n -> infinity' and eps_N -> 0 but does not say that N and n tend to infinity jointly.
issues.corrective_action: In the sentence after (8), list what Proposition 3 needs for SDLC: uniform consistency of mu_hat, sigma_hat and g_hat; sigma bounded below by a constant above the floor, or a floor that is o(1); and a domain D_N whose complement has vanishing probability. In Proposition 3 write 'N, n -> infinity'. Optionally weaken the assumption to |f_hat(Y|X) - f(Y|X)| -> 0 in probability for the threshold step and E_X sup_y|f_hat - f| -> 0 for the set step; the proof goes through with an extra term for the fraction of badly estimated calibration scores and the bound |C*(x) \ D_N| <= P(Y not in D_N | X=x)/min_k t_k. Mention that the floor may explain the socmob loss.

issues.title: Highlight 2 still overclaims coverage of extreme outcomes (cycle-1 fix C1-03 incomplete)
issues.evidence: highlights_filled.md: 'Calibrating within target strata guarantees coverage of rare, extreme outcomes'. The guarantee (5) is a stratum average. The Appendix Remark shows that within a tail stratum coverage decreases towards the outer end even for the oracle, and Table 2 reports SDLC top-1% coverage of 0.736 (S-NCP 0.789; all methods below 0.9). response_01.md C1-03 says the highlights 'no longer claim extreme-outcome superiority', but this highlight still promises a guarantee for 'extreme outcomes'.
issues.corrective_action: Reword to, for example: 'Calibrating within target strata guarantees average coverage within each target stratum, such as the top decile' (85 characters or fewer, as ESWA requires).

issues.title: Precision gaps in Theorem 1 and in the 'price' remark
issues.evidence: (a) Theorem 1 says 'The levels alpha_k may depend on n_k', but (5) and the marginal bound 1 - sum_k p_k alpha_k are stated unconditionally on n_k. If alpha_k = alpha_k(n_k), the right-hand side of (5) is random. The proof in fact gives the bound conditional on n_k. (b) The 'price of stratum-wise validity' paragraph says the stratified and marginal optima 'coincide if and only if t_1=...=t_K'. Under Proposition 2's assumptions alone (continuous, not strictly increasing distribution of f(Y|X) given B_k), the thresholds t_k need not be unique, so the 'only if' direction fails as stated. The second formulation in the same sentence ('iff that marginal set already has coverage 1-alpha_k in every stratum') is correct.
issues.corrective_action: (a) State (5) conditional on n_k when the levels depend on n_k, or restrict the marginal statement to fixed levels. (b) Add 'and the thresholds are unique (as under the assumption of Proposition 3)', or keep only the coverage-based characterisation.

issues.title: Small wording inaccuracies about the estimator and about exchangeability
issues.evidence: (a) Section 4.3: SDLC-N uses a normal density 'with the same defensive component'. GaussianNoiseDensity (density.py lines 177-189) uses a t2 component with scale s_t = 1, not IQR/1.349 of the residuals. (b) Section 4.3 says that with cross-fitting 'neither mu_hat nor sigma_hat has seen the residual it standardises'. In refit_scales.py lines 52-62, the scale model for fold j is trained on |r_a| for a != j, and those r_a come from mean models mu_hat_{-a} that were trained on fold j's data, so Y_j enters indirectly. (c) Section 6.8 ('Repeated units'): 'Theorem 1 assumes exchangeable rows, which such data violate'. Under random row splits the rows are exchangeable and Theorem 1 holds for a random row of the dataset; it is the grouped (unit-level) split that breaks row-level exchangeability between calibration and test data. (d) Section 6.7: 'Every stratified method guarantees an alert recall of at least 0.9', but Table 9 includes SDLC-floor, whose guarantee is 1-beta = 0.8.
issues.corrective_action: (a) Write 'with a defensive t2 component of unit scale'. (b) Write 'no scale model has been trained on the residual it standardises (the residuals of other folds depend on fold j only through the out-of-fold mean models)'. (c) Write 'Theorem 1 guarantees coverage for a randomly drawn row; for new units, calibration must be exchangeable at the level of units'. (d) Exclude SDLC-floor from that sentence, or state its 0.8 guarantee.

result.summary:
The comparison is fair and the protocol is mostly sound. Every method is evaluated from the same cached LightGBM outputs (experiments/evaluate_from_cache3.py build_context): S-NCP and SDLC use the same floored sigma-hat, CQR and S-CQR refit their quantile models for each alpha, and DCP, HPD-split, S-HPD and DLS share SDLC's location-scale density, so those comparisons isolate the calibration rule. BCCP, S-NCP, S-CQR, S-HPD, Mondrian-yhat, DCP and HPD-split are implemented faithfully.

I checked the confirmatory replication in detail:
- **Dataset list.** Through the OpenML API I fetched suites 335 and 336 (36 datasets). Every dataset is accounted for: 17 included, 9 removed for content overlap, 5 duplicate versions, 2 removed by the distinct-value rule, and cpu_act, houses and abalone also removed for overlap.
- **Primary analysis.** I re-ran the frozen pre-registration version of scripts/analyze_confirmatory.py (git archive ccba99b) on results/confirmatory/raw_eval_v3. It reproduces every reported C-H1 to C-H4 statistic exactly: C-H3 geometric-mean ratios 0.862, 0.977, 0.841 and 0.984 with Holm p 0.0011, 0.0077, 0.0006 and 0.0077; C-H2 1 of 17 against a critical value of 3. The only later change in its dependency src/statistics/tests.py is NaN handling, which has no effect here. The primary analysis was therefore run as pre-registered.

Three problems need fixing before submission, and none needs more than minutes of CPU:
1. **Decision study.** The claim that set-based alerts are cheaper when misses are very costly is an artefact of a fixed operating point (recall 0.9 for TC-LS), and the obvious cost-aware rule is missing. My seed-0 computation shows that this rule clearly beats SDLC alerts.
2. **Unreported secondary outcomes.** Pre-registered secondary outcomes are not reported, including an unfavourable one: on the held-out data SDLC-hull is not smaller than S-NCP-hull.
3. **Wording of the pre-registration.** "Pre-registered" and "made public before evaluation" cannot be verified as written. They contradict "will be deposited upon acceptance" and the paper's own definition of pre-registration in Section 5.7, and Supplement S6 prints an internal branch name.

Smaller fixes:
- An overclaiming highlight and an off-by-one method count in the abstract.
- The unqualified BCCP label (a cycle-1 fix that was only partly done).
- A "positive control" that is an arithmetic identity.
- A small fidelity issue in conformal selection.
- Rendering defects in p-value statements.

No essential baseline is missing for the main size and coverage claims.

issues.title: Decision study: operating-point confounding and a missing cost-aware baseline make the alert-cost conclusions unsupported
issues.evidence:
experiments/tail_alerts.py fixes ALPHA = 0.1 for TC-LS and TC-H (recall target 0.9) and compares them with SDLC alerts, whose realised recall is 0.978 (Table 9), at cost ratios r = 10 and 20. The rules are compared at different operating points that do not depend on r. The manuscript's own tests (tables/T13b_alert_tests.md) do not support the conclusion:
- r=20, SDLC vs TC-LS: 22/9, p = 0.083 (r=10: 14/17, p = 0.130).
- At r=20, marginal HPD-split alerts are cheaper than SDLC on 28/31 datasets and S-NCP alerts on 29/31 (both p < 0.001).
- In tables/T14_case_study.md at r=20, the cheapest rules for cps88wages are CQR (0.617), TC-LS (0.626) and SCP (0.633); SDLC costs 0.797 and S-NCP 0.767. For Miami the cheapest is HPD-split (0.075), against SDLC 0.080.
Stratified rules come out cheapest only at r=50 in Fig. 6.
My read-only computation on seed 0 (31 datasets; cached outputs in results/raw_contexts and raw_contexts_v3, scratch script, no files modified) used the plug-in cost-sensitive rule 'alert if P_hat(Y in B_K | x) > 1/(1+r)' from the same location-scale model that TC-LS uses:
- r=10: mean expected cost 0.216 against 0.297 for SDLC; SDLC cheaper on 2/31 datasets.
- r=20: 0.279 against 0.315; SDLC cheaper on 6/31.
The point rule and marginal-set alerts, which also have no guarantee, are already in Table 9, so this rule is an admissible baseline.
The following statements are therefore not supported: Section 6.7 ('set-based alerts with stratum-wise coverage are the cheapest at the highest ratios'), Section 7.2 item 5 ('Set-based alerts ... are cheaper when misses are very costly') and the Conclusion ('set-based alerts are cheaper when missed extremes are very costly').
issues.corrective_action:
Add two rows to Table 9 and Fig. 6: (a) the cost-aware plug-in rule P_hat > 1/(1+r) for each r, and (b) TC-LS with its recall level set per cost ratio, for example alpha_TC in {0.05, 0.02}, or a recall level matched to SDLC's realised recall. Report paired tests against SDLC. Then rewrite:
- Section 6.7, Section 7.2 item 5 and the Conclusion, saying that for yes/no decisions a classifier thresholded for the cost ratio dominates alerts read off sets. The case for sets is the extra information they carry, not the expected cost of alerts.
- The sentence about Fig. 6, which should say that stratified rules are cheapest only at r = 50, and only against fixed-recall rules.
Also state that S-NCP alerts are cheaper than SDLC alerts at every r, including r = 10 (3/27).
issues.new_experiment: Cache-only computation, a few CPU-minutes, no refits. Extend experiments/tail_alerts.py with rules 'Bayes-r' (alert iff sc_t > 1/(1+r), r in {1, 5, 10, 20, 50}) and TC-LS at alpha in {0.05, 0.02}, for 31 datasets x 10 seeds, both sides. Recompute alerts_study in scripts/analyze3.py and Fig. F13 with paired Wilcoxon tests (Holm within each r) of SDLC against each new rule. The locally available raw_contexts holds only seed-0 caches, so this needs the full v2 cache that tail_alerts.py used (or a refit with run_all.py).

issues.title: Pre-registered secondary outcomes of the confirmatory study are not reported, including an unfavourable hull result
issues.evidence:
PREREGISTRATION_confirmatory.md §4 lists as secondary outcomes: upper-tail, top-5% and top-1% coverage, the empty-set rate, worst sigma-hat-decile coverage, the C-H3 comparisons under S10, and the hull variants. §5 promises they will be reported 'whatever their direction'.
- Section 6.5 reports only top-1% coverage, the worst sigma-decile and the price. The supplement has no confirmatory results table: results/confirmatory/tables/C2_main.md and statistics_confirmatory.json 'C-H3_S10_descriptive' are not rendered anywhere.
- From results/confirmatory/raw_eval_v3, using the same per-dataset aggregation and paired_summary as the pre-registered script, SDLC-hull vs S-NCP-hull has a geometric-mean ratio of 1.040 [0.980, 1.144], HL ratio 0.996, 10/7, Wilcoxon p = 0.71. SDLC-hull vs BCCP-hull is 0.893, 13/4, p = 0.007.
- C2_main shows SDLC sets with 2.015 pieces on average, against 1.690 for S-NCP and 1.837 for BCCP.
- Section 7.2 item 4 ('SDLC-hull is valid and remains smaller than BCCP-hull, but it loses part of the advantage') rests on CTR23 only and omits that, on held-out data, SDLC-hull has no advantage over S-NCP-hull.
issues.corrective_action: Add a supplementary table, for example 'Confirmatory replication: secondary outcomes', that renders C2_main (all 17 methods, including SDLC-hull, BCCP-hull and S-NCP-hull) together with the paired hull comparisons and the S10 descriptive comparisons from statistics_confirmatory.json. Add one sentence to Section 6.5: on held-out data, SDLC-hull is smaller than BCCP-hull (0.893, 13/4) but not than S-NCP-hull (1.040, 10/7, p = 0.71), and SDLC sets have more pieces (2.02 vs 1.69). Revise Section 7.2 item 4 so that it recommends S-NCP-hull when an interval is mandatory. Compute the paired hull tests in a separate, clearly labelled script so that the frozen analyze_confirmatory.py stays unchanged.

issues.title: The terms 'pre-registered' and 'made public before evaluation' are unverifiable and inconsistent with the paper's own standard
issues.evidence:
- 01_intro.md and the cover letter say the analysis plan 'was made public before evaluation'. 03_setup.md:60 says it was 'committed it to the public repository'. Yet 07_declarations.md:15 says the code 'will be deposited in a public repository [repository URL] upon acceptance', so a reader cannot verify any 'public' commit.
- Section 5.7 refuses the label 'pre-registered' for the main benchmark because its expectations 'were not registered with a third party'. The confirmatory plan was not registered with a third party either. It sits in the authors' own git history; git timestamps are set by the author.
- Supplement S6 (supplementary_filled.md:510) prints the internal branch name 'claude/amazing-maxwell-i1mihd'.
- The pre-registration commit ccba99b also added partial v3 CTR23 evaluation files (results/raw_eval_v3/44963_*.jsonl, 44964_*.jsonl, ...), so the plan was written after part of the final-implementation CTR23 results existed. This does not invalidate the held-out test but should be disclosed.
- src/statistics/tests.py, which the frozen script imports, changed after ccba99b (Holm NaN handling, n<3 guard). I verified that the ccba99b version of the script reproduces all reported confirmatory statistics exactly, so the change is harmless.
issues.corrective_action:
Before submission, choose one of two routes:
- (a) Make the repository, with its full history, public now and archive it on Software Heritage or Zenodo, so that commit ccba99b and its timestamp can be checked independently. Cite the commit hash and archive DOI in Section 5.7 and S6.
- (b) Replace 'pre-registered' and 'made public before evaluation' throughout (abstract, highlights, intro, Section 5.7, Section 6.5, Table 7 caption, conclusion, cover letter) with 'analysis plan and script fixed and time-stamped in version control (commit ccba99b) before any confirmatory evaluation'.
In either case:
- Remove the branch name from S6.
- Disclose that the plan was committed together with partial CTR23 v3 results.
- Add a sentence stating that a helper module changed after the plan was frozen, and that re-running the frozen version reproduces every number.

issues.title: Headline wording overclaims and the BCCP label is still unqualified (incomplete fix of C1-02 items 1 and 3)
issues.evidence:
- Highlight 4 reads 'SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets on 31 datasets, confirmed on 17'. It was smallest only on average. SDLC beat BCCP on 24/31, S-NCP on 27/31 and S-HPD on 28/31 datasets (Table 5). On the 9 datasets with n < 1600 it was 5/4 against S-NCP (geometric-mean ratio 1.050). On the 15 skewed datasets, Holm p = 0.127 against S-NCP and S-CQR.
- The abstract says SDLC 'was compared with 13 procedures'. MAIN in scripts/analyze3.py:56 (n_methods_main = 13) includes SDLC-LS itself, so SDLC was compared with 12; the intro's 'we compare 13 conformal procedures' is correct.
- Review C1-02 asked for the headline BCCP comparison to be named 'BCCP with the absolute-residual score' and for the text to note that BCCP's reference implementation (pintervals) also offers a heteroscedastic score that is essentially S-NCP. The abstract still says 'smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction on 24 of 31 datasets'. grep finds no mention of the reference implementation's heteroscedastic option. Against the S-NCP-like variant the gain is only about 2-3% (0.975 CTR23, 0.977 held-out).
issues.corrective_action:
- Highlight 4: 'SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets on average (31 datasets), confirmed on 17 held-out'.
- Abstract: 'compared with 12 other procedures'.
- Abstract: 'smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction with the absolute-residual score on 24 of 31 datasets'.
- Sections 2.2 and 5.4: one sentence noting that BCCP is score-agnostic and that its reference implementation also offers a scale-normalised residual, which corresponds to S-NCP here, the comparator against which the gain is small.

issues.title: The 'positive control' for target shift is an arithmetic identity, not an empirical check
issues.evidence: evaluate_from_cache3.py shift_weights3 multiplies the importance weight of every test point in the upper stratum by 5 and in the lower stratum by 0.5. The test set is fixed and nothing is recalibrated. Weights that are constant within each stratum leave the within-stratum coverage of any method unchanged by construction. Table 8 shows this for every method: the positive-control worst stratum equals the Table 2 value, for example SCP 0.630, DLS 0.660 and SDLC 0.891. Section 6.6 nevertheless writes that 'the stratum-wise coverage of every stratified method was unchanged, as Corollary 1(i) states', which reads as empirical confirmation, and RQ4 and Section 5.5 call it a 'positive control'.
issues.corrective_action: Reword Sections 5.5 and 6.6: under whole-stratum re-weighting, stratum-wise coverage is unchanged for every method by definition. The informative quantity is the marginal coverage under the shift (stratified 0.904-0.906 against marginal 0.838-0.877), which follows from the stratum-wise guarantee. Drop the claim that this verifies Corollary 1(i), or keep only the remark that it illustrates the corollary. Also state in Section 5.5 that all tilts re-weight a fixed test set, while the genuine label shift appears only in the synthetic study (Table S10).

issues.title: Conformal-selection baseline uses null-only p-value denominators, unlike its docstring and Jin & Candès
issues.evidence: The docstring of conformal_pvalues in experiments/tail_alerts.py says 'the denominator uses the whole calibration set'. The code divides by len(s_null_cal)+1, about 0.9 n, which makes every p-value about 11% larger, so BH runs at an effective level of about q/1.11. On seed 0 (31 datasets, read-only recomputation), CS-BH-0.2 mean upper-tail recall is 0.629 as coded and 0.641 with the full-calibration denominator. The effect is small but slightly weakens a baseline.
issues.corrective_action: Use (len(s_cal)+1) in the denominator, as in Jin & Candès' clipped-score p-value, or correct the docstring and state in Section 5.4 that p-values are computed against null calibration units only (valid but conservative). Re-run tail_alerts.py, which takes minutes.

issues.evidence:
In manuscript_filled.md:
- Line 272 (twice) and line 310: '$p\le$ < 0.001'. The template writes '$p\le$ {{...}}' and the placeholder already contains '< 0.001'.
- Line 462: 'Holm $p$ < 0.001 or smaller'.

Format the C-H4 median differences so that negative zero prints as 0.0000 (for example -1.4e-5 shown as '< 0.0001 in absolute value').

result.summary:
I checked the statistics against statistics_v3.json and statistics_confirmatory.json. Every headline inferential number in the manuscript matches the result files, so the core inference is sound. Specifically:
- Holm adjustments recomputed by hand: H1 families of 7, H3 primary family of 4, decomposition family of 3, hull family of 2, extreme-coverage family of 16.
- Sign tests, Hodges-Lehmann (HL) ratios and geometric-mean bootstrap CIs match.
- TOST p-values (margin 0.01 on CTR23, 0.02 on held-out data) match.
- The C-H2 binomial critical value (3 for Binomial(17, 0.05)) and the C-H3 decision rule are implemented as written.
- The unit of analysis is the dataset, and one-sided tests are used only for H1, as stated.
- Since the plan commit ccba99b, analyze_confirmatory.py is unchanged. Only cosmetic changes were made to tests.py (NaN handling) and refit_scales.py (task listing).

The remaining problems concern reporting completeness and claim accuracy rather than arithmetic, but a hostile referee will find several of them:
1. The confirmatory study is called "pre-registered" under a standard the paper itself rejects in Section 5.7. The repository is described both as "public" and as to be made public "upon acceptance".
2. Pre-registered secondary analyses that are unfavourable to SDLC are not reported. On held-out data, SDLC-hull is larger than S-NCP-hull (geometric-mean ratio 1.04, 10/7 datasets).
3. Worst-slab coverage (WSC) is promised in Section 5.5 and was requested in cycle 1, but is never reported. SDLC is lower than S-NCP on 20/27 datasets (p = 0.0003).
4. The scale-decile evidence shown is the non-significant summary, while the strong, two-sided reallocation pattern is not shown.
5. One sentence about the ESS >= 50 shift subset is false.
6. Highlights 2 and 4 overstate the results.
7. Where the bootstrap CI of the geometric mean includes 1, the "smaller" claims against S-NCP rest on a skewed signed-rank test, without the promised sign-test column.

All fixes can be done from existing result files in a few hours; no new experiment is needed.

issues.title: "Pre-registered" label for the confirmatory replication cannot be verified and contradicts the paper's own standard and its data statement
issues.evidence:
The paper applies two standards to the same kind of evidence.
- For CTR23, Section 5.7 (manuscript_filled.md line ~240) says the configuration was committed to version control but "These expectations were not registered with a third party, and we do not call the study pre-registered."
- The confirmatory plan is equally a git commit (ccba99b, 2026-11-18 09:49:14, branch claude/amazing-maxwell-i1mihd), with no third-party registry. Yet the label "pre-registered" appears in the abstract, Highlight 4 (implicitly), Section 6.5, the Table 7 caption, Section 7.1, the Conclusion, Supplementary S6 and the cover letter.

The repository's public status is also stated inconsistently:
- Supplementary S6 (line 506) and PREREGISTRATION_confirmatory.md say the plan was "committed to the public repository".
- The Data and code availability statement (line ~530) says code "will be deposited in a public repository [repository URL] upon acceptance".
- The cover letter says the plan "was made public before evaluation".

Git author timestamps are set by the committer and cannot be verified by a referee. The cycle-1 corrective action (C1-01 item 1) was to keep "pre-registered" only with a verifiable public snapshot; that fix is therefore inadequate for the confirmatory study. The timeline is otherwise plausible: confirmatory raw_eval_v3 first appears in commit c3cad49 at 10:10, after ccba99b.
issues.corrective_action:
1. Pick one of two wordings and use it everywhere.
   (a) If the plan was in fact on a public, third-party-timestamped host before evaluation (a public GitHub push, Software Heritage or Zenodo record), cite that URL or DOI and the timestamp in Section 5.7 and S6.
   (b) Otherwise, replace "pre-registered" with "analysis plan fixed in advance (version-controlled commit ccba99b, timestamp 2026-11-18 09:49 UTC, before any confirmatory evaluation; not registered with a third party)". Apply this in the abstract, Section 6.5 and its heading text, the Table 7 caption, Section 7.1, the Conclusion, S6 and the cover letter. This is the same standard Section 5.7 applies to CTR23.
2. Remove "public" from S6 and PREREGISTRATION_confirmatory.md unless (a) holds.
3. Make the cover letter consistent with the data statement.
4. Disclose in S6 that tests.py (NaN-safe holm/paired_summary) and refit_scales.py (task enumeration) changed after the plan commit, and say why this does not affect the results. Also state why the equivalence margin is 0.02 here but 0.01 in Section 6.3.

issues.title: Pre-registered secondary analyses are omitted from the manuscript, including an unfavourable hull result and the S10 comparisons, and the script deviates from the plan
issues.evidence:
PREREGISTRATION_confirmatory.md Section 4 lists these secondary analyses: price vs DLS; upper-tail, top-5% and top-1% coverage; empty-set rate; worst sigma-decile coverage; "the C-H3 comparisons under decile strata (S10)"; and "hull variants". Section 5 promises they will be reported "whatever their direction". Section 6.5 reports only top-1% coverage, worst sigma-decile coverage and the price.

Omitted:
- **Hull variants.** results/confirmatory/statistics_confirmatory.json summary gives size_geo 1.363 for SDLC-hull and 1.311 for S-NCP-hull. I seed-averaged the S5, alpha = 0.1 runs in results/confirmatory/raw_eval_v3 (without the modal-K filter). SDLC-hull / S-NCP-hull has a geometric-mean ratio of 1.040, is smaller on only 10/17 datasets, and the two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.71. SDLC-hull / BCCP-hull: 0.893, 13/4, p = 0.007.
- **S10 comparisons.** statistics_confirmatory.json 'C-H3_S10_descriptive' exists (SDLC/S-NCP 0.988, 14/3) but is not reported anywhere.
- **Deviation from the plan.** analyze_confirmatory.py computes S10 comparisons only for ("S-Res", "S-NCP", "S-CQR") and omits S-HPD, although the plan says "the C-H3 comparisons", meaning all four comparators.
- **Empty-set rate** (SDLC 0.0003 vs S-NCP 0.0) is not reported.
- **No per-dataset table.** No per-dataset confirmatory size table is in the supplement, although tables/C3_per_dataset_size.csv exists.

Section 7.2 item 4 still says SDLC-hull "loses part of the advantage". On held-out data it has none against S-NCP-hull, and on CTR23 its geometric-mean ratio is 1.014.

issues.title: Worst-slab coverage is promised in Section 5.5 and requested in cycle 1, but never reported; it is clearly unfavourable to SDLC
issues.evidence:
Section 5.5 (line 227) lists "worst-slab coverage (WSC) [@cauchois2021knowing]" as a metric. Cycle-1 C1-04 item 3 asked for Holm-tested WSC differences among stratified methods. The response to C1-04 reports sigma-decile coverage and empty sets but is silent on WSC. WSC appears only as an unlabelled column in Supplementary Table S9 (variants only); it is absent from Table 2 and from the main text.

From results/per_dataset_main_v3.csv (column wsc, 27 datasets with a value):

| Comparison | Mean WSC | SDLC lower on | Two-sided Wilcoxon p (unadjusted) | Sign-test p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SDLC vs S-NCP | 0.848 vs 0.887 | 20/27 | 0.0003 | 0.019 |
| SDLC vs S-HPD | 0.848 vs 0.884 | 22/27 | 0.001 | 0.0015 |

issues.title: Sigma-decile evidence: the statistic reported is not significant, while the decisive two-sided reallocation pattern goes unreported
issues.evidence:
Section 6.3 and Fig. 4 give "The worst coverage over deciles of sigma-hat(x) was 0.769 for SDLC against 0.793 for S-NCP", and the abstract says gains "came with lower coverage of the noisiest inputs". Per dataset (results/per_dataset_main_v3.csv, sig_worst), SDLC is lower on only 17 of 31 datasets (two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.49), so the reported statistic gives no evidence of a difference.

The actual pattern, from seed-averaged sig_cov_9 / sig_cov_0 in raw_eval_v3 (alpha = 0.1, S5, full calibration):

| sigma-hat decile | SDLC | S-NCP | SDLC lower on | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Top (noisiest) | 0.818 | 0.936 | 31/31 | < 1e-6 |
| Bottom (quietest) | 0.900 | 0.836 | 0/31 (higher on 31/31) | < 1e-6 |

Held-out data, top decile: 0.832 vs 0.932, lower on 17/17.

This is exactly the reallocation that the Section 4.3 remark predicts, and it is far larger than the worst-decile difference shown. S-NCP under-covers the quietest inputs to the same extent that SDLC under-covers the noisiest. The current text overstates SDLC's cost on the worst-decile metric and understates it on the top decile.

issues.title: The "smaller than S-NCP" claims rest on a signed-rank test of strongly skewed log ratios; the promised sign-test column and the requested size TOST are missing
issues.evidence:
Section 5.6 says size comparisons are summarised with the numbers of wins and losses and the sign test. Table 5, Table S5 and Table 7 show only Wilcoxon Holm p; the sign-test p (p_sign in statistics_v3.json) is never printed.

For SDLC vs S-NCP the 95% bootstrap CI of the geometric-mean ratio, the stated primary summary, includes 1 in most analyses:

| Analysis | GM ratio [95% CI] |
|---|---|
| Primary | 0.975 [0.941, 1.020] |
| Excl. development | [0.940, 1.027] |
| Excl. development + diagnostic | [0.930, 1.037] |
| alpha = 0.05 | 0.990 [0.951, 1.047] |
| S3 | [0.922, 1.008] |
| S10 | [0.950, 1.023] |
| Held out (C-H3) | [0.940, 1.028] |
| Held out, S-HPD | [0.963, 1.014] |

The per-dataset log ratios are strongly right-skewed: scipy.stats.skew = 2.79, driven by socmob +0.493 and cars +0.181 (computed from per_dataset_main_v3.csv). Under skewness the signed-rank test can reject because of asymmetry rather than a shift. Its location estimate is the pseudo-median (HL 0.962), not the geometric mean. The sign test (27/4, p = 3.4e-5) supports "smaller on most datasets" robustly, but it is not shown.

The Wilcoxon and sign tests also disagree elsewhere:
- alert rate SDLC vs S-NCP: Wilcoxon p = 0.0175 (Holm 0.035), sign test p = 0.36 (12/18);
- hull vs S-NCP-hull: Wilcoxon Holm p = 0.034 with geometric mean 1.014.

The cycle-1 C1-02 item 4 TOST for size equivalence (margin ±5%) was neither reported nor declined. Computed with tests.tost_wilcoxon on log ratios, margin log(1.05): p = 0.145 on CTR23 and 0.054 held out, so neither a difference in mean nor equivalence is established.

The bootstrap CIs are percentile intervals (tests.bootstrap_ci). Cycle-1 C1-30(b) asked for BCa for geometric-mean ratios, which matters given this skewness.

1. Add a "Sign p (Holm)" column to Table 5, Table S5 and Table 7, and to the alert-rate statement in Section 6.7. Adjust the sign tests by Holm within the same families.
2. Word every S-NCP/S-HPD size claim as "smaller on most datasets (median/HL ratio X; sign test p)", noting that the geometric-mean CI includes 1, as Section 6.5 already does. Apply this in Section 6.3's first paragraph, the robustness paragraph and Section 6.8.
3. Report the ±5% TOST result for SDLC vs S-NCP (p = 0.145 CTR23; 0.054 held out) in one sentence, or state explicitly that it was not done and why.
4. Switch the geometric-mean CIs to BCa (scipy.stats.bootstrap with method='BCa'), or justify the percentile interval. Re-running analyze3.py takes minutes.

issues.title: The null reference treats seeds as independent and is applied to floor variants at the wrong level
issues.evidence:
null_worst_stratum (code/scripts/analyze.py lines 107-135) draws an independent Beta-binomial coverage per seed and averages over seeds. The 10 seeds are re-partitions of the same finite dataset, so calibration-conditional coverages are positively correlated across seeds. The null spread of the seed-average is therefore underestimated, and the 5% quantile is too high (anti-conservative for flagging).

This does not threaten the stratified conclusions (1-2 of 31 flagged; 1 of 17 held out), but the method should be described as an approximation.

Table S9 reports "n_ds_below_null" of 28, 23 and 29 for BCCP-floor, S-NCP-floor and SDLC-floor. These variants target 1 - beta = 0.8 in the tail strata but are compared with a 1 - alpha null, which suggests they are invalid.
issues.corrective_action:
1. In Section 5.5, state that the null assumes independent splits and is therefore approximate (conservative for claiming validity).
2. Optionally add a sensitivity null that resamples whole seeds (or uses the empirical seed-to-seed variance of the stratified methods).
3. In Table S9, compute the null for floor variants at their nominal per-stratum level, or show "n/a" with a footnote.
